images.caption: Figure 1:Three context-management paradigms for long-horizon world generation.Dense chunked generation keeps an ever-growing visual context. Frame-memory methods retrieve a small set of past views using camera overlap. Velox routes each current latent region to compact, geometry-relevant history blocks using frustum slab correspondences.

Figure 2:Velox overview.Velox leaves the pretrained chunked video generator unchanged and replaces dense historical attention with frustum slab routed attention. Historical chunks are summarized by per-block frustum slabs with depth intervals, target query blocks obtain depth through multiwarp, and block routes softly fuse frustum slab overlap with layer-specific model importance before adding temporal and global Gilbert safeguards. Indexed sparse attention then produces the next chunk.

Figure 4:Qualitative comparison with dense attention.For each case, we show the shared input frame, followed by dense LingBot-Fast-Cam (top row) and Velox (bottom row) at25%25\%,50%50\%,75%75\%, and100%100\%of the rollout. Both models receive the same input frame and camera trajectory, and timestamps are given in seconds. The two rollouts are similar early on. In later frames, dense attention drifts away from the input, as the bedroom is replaced by an unrelated dark room, the figurine fades to pale pink, the bamboo path degrades into a puddle and then a featureless surface, and dark artifacts spread across the dunes. Velox remains consistent with the input frame and preserves fine appearance details through the end of the rollout. Cases are selected for illustration, and Table1reports aggregate quality.

Figure 5:Additional qualitative comparisons.Same protocol as Figure4. Dense attention smears texture and distorts the subject in the beach case, loses the crowd and ends on a blurred surface in the subway case, and turns the cobblestone path into a puddle in the gnome case. Velox stays closer to the input frame in all three cases.
